query: Identify a processing route and property optimization strategy for a lightweight, multi-principal element alloy system. The goal is to achieve high density and hardness while ensuring resistance to high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion. Request a hypothesis for the material composition and processing method, supporting evidence on phase stability, boundary conditions for the processing temperature, and a falsification experiment to test the mechanism of property enhancement.

generation.hypothesis: A quaternary CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy modified with 5 at.% Tungsten (W) and 3 at.% Aluminum (Al), processed via powder metallurgy followed by a two-stage heat treatment (solutionizing at 1100°C followed by aging at 700°C), will simultaneously achieve high density, high hardness, and superior oxidation/corrosion resistance through the formation of a coherent B2-NiAl precipitate network and a W-enriched passive oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder mixture of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, W, and Al elemental powders with a nominal composition of Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20W5Al3 (at.%), characterized by a nanocrystalline solid solution structure (FCC/BCC mixture) after high-energy ball milling, similar to the 83% FCC/17% BCC structure observed in CoCrFeNiTi alloys [PMC12298864::chunk::000::abstract::934a070a39].
generation.intervention: Consolidation via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1050°C under 50 MPa, followed by a solution heat treatment at 1100°C for 1 hour in vacuum, and a subsequent aging treatment at 700°C for 10 hours.
generation.conditions: Processing atmosphere: High vacuum (<10^-3 Pa) for sintering and solutionizing; Aging in inert Argon. Testing environment: 800°C air for oxidation, 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25°C for corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nano-scale, coherent B2-ordered NiAl intermetallic phase precipitating within the FCC matrix, coupled with the segregation of Tungsten to the grain boundaries and the formation of a Cr2O3/Al2O3 dual-layer passive film.
generation.mechanism: The W addition stabilizes the B2 phase and increases stacking fault energy, while the Al promotes the formation of a protective alumina scale [PMC6197204::chunk::000::abstract::a6951d7e3c]. The aging treatment drives the precipitation of B2-NiAl, which acts as a potent barrier to dislocation motion (hardness) and impedes oxygen diffusion (oxidation resistance), while the W-enriched grain boundaries prevent intergranular corrosion. The formation of protective oxide layers (Cr2O3, Al2O3) is critical for corrosion resistance in oxidative environments [PMC6908586::chunk::001::introduction::7b08936e5e].
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will exhibit a Vickers hardness > 500 HV, a density > 8.5 g/cm³, an oxidation mass gain < 0.5 mg/cm² after 100 hours at 800°C, and a corrosion current density < 1 µA/cm² in 3.5% NaCl, outperforming the unaged CoCrFeNi baseline.
generation.baseline: The unmodified Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20 alloy (Cantor alloy) processed under identical SPS conditions without W and Al additions, which typically exhibits lower hardness (~250 HV) and forms a less protective Cr2O3 scale prone to spallation at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the aging temperature remains below 750°C to prevent the formation of brittle sigma phases; if the W content exceeds 8 at.%, the formation of topologically close-packed (TCP) phases may dominate, degrading toughness and corrosion resistance. The phase stability is highly dependent on the combination of composition and annealing temperature [PMC6197204::chunk::000::abstract::a6951d7e3c].
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact kinetics of B2 precipitation during the specific cooling rates of SPS; if the cooling rate is too fast, the B2 phase may not nucleate sufficiently, leading to lower hardness than predicted. Additionally, the long-term stability of the W-enriched grain boundary film in aggressive chloride environments is less documented compared to Cr/Al oxides.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiW5Al3 samples: Set A undergoes the proposed two-stage heat treatment (1100°C/1h + 700°C/10h), while Set B is quenched directly from 1100°C to room temperature (no aging). Both sets are subjected to 800°C oxidation for 100 hours and electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify B2 phase fraction
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) with EDS to analyze oxide scale thickness and composition
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to determine corrosion resistance
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to observe precipitate coherence and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Set B (quenched) exhibits a hardness within 10% of Set A (aged) OR if the oxide scale on Set A is thicker or less adherent than that of Set B, indicating that the B2 precipitation does not contribute to the predicted property enhancement.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] .
